title: Nerve and muscle test (EMG)
what: The doctor checks how signals travel along your nerves and how your muscles work. Sensors on the skin, weak electrical pulses, and sometimes a thin needle are used.
why: For numbness, tingling, or weakness in your arms or legs, after nerve injuries, for back pain that spreads to the leg, or with diabetes.
tell_doctor: If you have a pacemaker or another device in your body
Blood thinner medicines, if a needle test is planned
If you have swelling or a skin disease on your arms or legs

prepare.title: Skin
prepare.text: Wash your arms and legs. Do not use cream or oil on the day of the test.

prepare.title: Warmth
prepare.text: Cold hands and feet change the result. Come in warm clothes and socks.

prepare.title: Clothes
prepare.text: Wear loose clothes, so your arms and legs are easy to uncover. Take off rings and bracelets.

prepare.title: Medicines
prepare.text: Do not stop your medicines. If you are unsure, tell your doctor. The doctor decides.

bring: Past EMG and MRI reports, if you have them
steps: You lie or sit down and uncover the arm or leg being tested
Sensors are stuck on your skin
The doctor sends short, weak electrical pulses to the nerve
A computer records how fast the signal travels
Sometimes a thin needle goes into a muscle, and you are asked to tense and relax it
feel: The pulses feel like clicks or small electric shocks. Unpleasant, but bearable
The muscle may twitch on its own. This is normal
The needle feels like a quick prick
after: You can go back to your day right away
After a needle test, the muscle may ache a little for a day or two
The report is given right away or in 1 to 2 days

faq.a: The pulses are unpleasant, like a small electric click, but short. Most people handle it calmly.

faq.q: Is the electric current in an EMG dangerous?
faq.a: No. The current is very weak and short. It only checks the nerve.
